title: "Estimation via Maximization"
format: beamer

## Switching Gears to Estimation

Now that we understand the basics of coding in ```R```, we're going to talk about estimating unknown parameters.

This material is based on the free textbook: [Core Statistics](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~swood34/core-statistics.pdf)

There are many approaches to parameter estimation, but we will focus on two:

- Estimation via **maximization**
- Estimation via **simulation**

## Estimation via Maximization

Examples of estimation via maximization include:

- Maximum likelihood estimation
- Method of moments estimation
- Loss function based estimators
- Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation

## Maximization vs. Minimization vs. Solving a System

We're going to treat all three as equivalent.

Maximizing something is the same as minimizing $-1$ times something.

Solving a system of equations is the same as minimizing absolute or squared deviations of the left hand sides and the right hand sides.

## Working Through an Example 

Consider some data:
```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}
t <- seq(2, 14, by = 1)
y <- c(35, 33, 33, 39, 24, 25, 
       18, 20, 23, 13, 14, 20, 18)
```

- ```y[i]``` represents the $i$-th count of cells in a culture
- ```t[i]``` describes hours since treatment of the culture with an antibiotic for the $i$-th count

## Always Visualize First

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
plot(t, y, pch = 16)
```

## What does maximum likelihood require?

A statistical model for the data, in this case ```y``` and ```t```.

The researchers want to fit the a model that describes the expected culture count as

$$E[y_i] = 50\times \text{exp}\left\{-\theta t_i\right\}$$

Where $50$ describes the count of cells in the culture before the antibiotic was administered and the parameter is $\theta$.

Is this a model?

## A Model for Our Data

We need to assume a distribution for each $y_i$ and we need to assume a dependence structure relating distinct elements of $y_i$ and to each other

We assume

$$y_i\stackrel{indep}{\sim}\text{Poisson}(50\times \text{exp}\left\{-\theta t_i\right\})$$

## Our First Likelihood

To start, let's pick a candidate value of $\theta$ to evaluate the likelihood at. 
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
theta0 <- 1
```

We can use the built in Poisson density function to obtain the likelihood for any observation, e.g.
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
dpois(y[1], 50*exp(-theta0*t[1]))
```

We obtain the likelihood for the complete data by taking the product...
```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
prod(dpois(y, 50*exp(-theta0*t)))
```

## Maximizing the Likelihood

Intuitively, we find the maximum by evaluating the likelihood at a set of candidate values for $\theta$ and identifying which value achieves the maximum likelihood.

For instance, we could evaluate the likelihood for values of $\theta$ between $0$ and $1$.

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
thetas <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)
ls <- rep(NA, length(thetas))
for (i in 1:length(thetas)) {
  ls[i] <- prod(dpois(y, 50*exp(-thetas[i]*t)))
}
```

## Maximizing the Likelihood
\footnotesize
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE} 
plot(thetas, ls, pch = 16)
```

## Working on the Log Scale

We can see that something a little weird is happening with our likelihood...
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
tail(ls)
```

The last several values are exactly $0$, because they correspond to products of many tiny (but not nonzero) numbers.

This motivates working on the log scale for maximum likelihood.

Finding the value that maximizes the log of a function $=$ finding the value that maximizes a function

## Maximizing the Log Likelihood

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
lls <- rep(NA, length(thetas))
for (i in 1:length(thetas)) {
  lls[i] <- sum(dpois(y, 50*exp(-thetas[i]*t), log = TRUE))
}
```

## Maximizing the Log-Likelihood
\footnotesize
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE, warning=FALSE} 
plot(thetas, lls, pch = 16)
abline(v = thetas[which.max(lls)], col = "blue", lty = 2)
```

## This is very inefficient!

The approach we just took does give us a sense of:

- Where the maximizing value is
- The shape of the likelihood

However, it:

- Gives an imprecise solution
- Requires specification of an interval to check

## Using ```optim```

In practice, we will use optimization algorithms to maximize likelihoods. 

In ```R```, the most basic way to do this uses ```optim```.

The ```optim``` function minimizes by default and requires:

- Starting values for the parameters that are being minimize over
- A function to minimize

## Creating a Log-Likelihood Function

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
ll <- function(theta, y, t) {
  -sum(dpois(y, 50*exp(-theta*t), log = TRUE))
}
```

Note: ```optim``` likes to have the parameter that will be minimized over specified first.

## Applying ```optim``` and Interpreting Output

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE, warning=TRUE}
opt <- optim(0.2, ll, y = y, t = t)
```

We do get a warning - but this is one that it can be ok to ignore and we will talk about why it's happening and ways around it.

## Interpreting ```optim```  Output

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
opt
```

## Our New Estimator
\footnotesize
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE, warning=FALSE} 
plot(thetas, lls, pch = 16)
abline(v = thetas[which.max(lls)], col = "blue", lty = 2)
abline(v = opt$par, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

## Getting Rid of the ```optim``` Error

The ```optim``` error arises when your unknown parameter is a **scalar**.

There are multiple ways to get rid of it but none use ```method="Nelder-Mead"```, with or without providing an interval to maximize over.

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE, warning=TRUE}
opt <- optim(0.2, ll, y = y, t = t, method = "BFGS")
opt <- optim(0.2, ll, y = y, t = t, method = "L-BFGS-B")
opt <- optim(0.2, ll, y = y, t = t, method = "CG")
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE, warning=TRUE}
opt <- optim(0.2, ll, y = y, t = t, method = "Brent", 
             lower = 0, upper = 1)
opt <- optimize(ll, y = y, t = t, lower = 0, upper = 1)
```

Check how they compare!

## What the heck are these methods?

Nelder-Mead, BFGS, L-BFGS-B, CG, and Brent all describe different algorithms for minimizing or maximizing a function, and which works best depends on the type of problem. 

In general, L-BFGS-B is most stable, especially when we have a parameter vector.

## What's an additional way we can check our solution?

We may want to verify that the gradient is in fact sufficiently close to $0$ at the maximum likelihood estimate of $\theta$.

What is the gradient? We need to write out the log likelihood and take a derivative with respect to $\theta$.

## Rewriting the Log-Likelihood

First, let's write out the log likelihood but in ```R``` so we can check our work.
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
llnew <- function(theta, y, t) {
  -sum(y*log(50) -y*theta*t +
         - 50*exp(-theta*t) - log(factorial(y)))
}
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
ll(theta0, y, t)
llnew(theta0, y, t)
```

## Defining a Gradient Function

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
llgrad <- function(theta, y, t) {
  -sum(-y*t + t*50*exp(-theta*t))
}
```

Examining the gradient function at candidate solutions
```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = TRUE}
llgrad(0.09377259, y = y, t = t)
llgrad(thetas[which.max(lls)], y = y, t = t)
```

## Modifying the Example to Have a Vector Parameter

Suppose we did not know the cell count before antibiotics were administered. 

Then we would consider
$$y_i\stackrel{indep}{\sim}\text{Poisson}(\theta_2\times \text{exp}\left\{-\theta_1 t_i\right\})$$


## Doing It Ourselves with Newton's Method

It can be helpful to work through an optimization algorithm ourselves.
